newsitem.title: USA: CFTC opposes realignment of U.S. trading rules.
newsitem.headline: CFTC opposes realignment of U.S. trading rules.

text.p: The federal regulator of U.S. futures markets said Tuesday that it opposed a Senate proposal aimed at clarifying the so-called Treasury amendment on foreign currency and government securities transactions.
Brooksley Born, head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said the bill would remove vital protection against fraud and manipulation by unscrupulous operators.
A Treasury official warned against overbroad regulation.
The agencies have disagreed for years over the Treasury amendment and there has been repeated litigation over it.
The Supreme Court heard arguments last fall whether the amendment blocked the CFTC from pursuing unscrupulous "bucket shops" if they deal in the several categories covered by the Treasury amendment.

A bill filed by Senate Agriculture Committee leaders would clarify that CFTC had jurisdiction over such sales to "retail investors, even if off-exchange unless another federal agency already supervised the sellers. Exchanges could offer unregulated products under the Treasuary amendment but only to institutional or sophisticated customers.

Born said the bill would remove most protections against fraud and manipulation at a time when "more regulatory power may be needed -- certainly not less." She cited 19 cases since 1990 against fraudulent off-exchange sales involving $250 million in foreign currency futures and options.

Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson said the argument for exempting foreign currency and government securities sales "from unnecessary regulation and uncertainty is, if anything, more compelling than it was in 1974."
CFTC and Treasury sent the committee differing proposals on the Treasury amendment. Months of negotiations have failed to arrive at a single proposal from the Clinton administration.

The President's Working Group on Financial Markets was scheduled to meet Tuesday to discuss the Treasury amendment. Chaired by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, the panel's members include CFTC, the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as White House agencies.

Treasury sought creation of the exemption in 1974 on grounds that the foreign currency market in the United States was composed of sophisticated players, such as banks and dealers, and most of them were already regulated.
"The Treasury is sympathetic to CFTC's enforcement concerns," Anderson said, but not "overbroad legislation."

In a joint statement, the seven largest U.S. futures exchanges said they viewed the Senate bill as "a fundamental shift in regulation of our markets and offers us a chance to compete with over-the-counter dealer markets and foreign exchanges on a playing field more level than we have ever enjoyed."
In particular, they praised the opportunity to create "professional markets" and asked for more opportunity to create new products for that forum.

The exchanges said the bill would result in different levels of protection for investors depending where they bought financial instruments. "While banks and broker-dealers are subject to a level of federal supervision or regulation, they do not provide safeguards comparable to the exchange trading environment," they said.

Senator Phil Gramm, Texas Republican, said he had reservations that the bill would lead to an explosion of CFTC regulatory power. Senator Bob Kerrey, Nebraska Democrat, said he was concerned whether the bill would strip newcomers to the currency markets of helpful protections.
Chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, said he hoped to report a bill to the floor by mid-year.
